Autocratic, paternalistic, democratic and laissez-faire styles differ in how far decision-making power is shared with employees.
A model placing leadership on a scale from manager-centred telling to subordinate-centred delegating, based on how much freedom staff are given.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Managers, Leadership and Decision Making — a core area of A-Level Business Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Managers, Leadership and Decision Making brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Managers, Leadership and Decision Making.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: In a decision tree, the expected value of an option is found by:
options: Multiplying each outcome's payoff by its probability and summing the results
Choosing the highest payoff regardless of probability
Adding all the payoffs and dividing by the costs
Always selecting the branch with the lowest cost
Makes decisions alone with little consultation
Delegates most decisions to the team
Seeks consensus before every decision
Avoids making any decisions at all

mcqs.q: Mendelow's matrix maps stakeholders according to their:
options: Power and interest
Profit and loss
Price and quality
Age and income

mcqs.q: Intuitive decision-making is most appropriate when:
options: Time is short, data is limited and the manager has deep experience
Large, reliable data sets are readily available
The decision is so high-risk that documented evidence is essential
Shareholders demand a fully data-driven process

mcqs.q: Is one leadership style always best?
options: No — the effective style depends on the situation: task urgency, the skill and experience of staff, and the culture; good leaders adapt their style.
Democratic leadership is always superior to autocratic leadership.
Leaders are elected by employees under company law.
UK companies must register their leadership style with Companies House.

mcqs.q: Do decision trees guarantee the right decision?
options: Leaders are elected by employees under company law.
Decision trees are only used by businesses in the forestry industry.
No — they clarify options and expected values, but probabilities and payoffs are estimates, and they ignore qualitative factors like morale and brand image.
Following the highest expected value branch ensures the best real outcome.

mcqs.q: Are managers and leaders the same thing?
options: Leaders are elected by employees under company law.
Anyone with a manager job title is automatically a leader.
Not exactly — management focuses on planning, organising and controlling resources, while leadership is about setting direction and inspiring people; one person may do both.
Decision trees are only used by businesses in the forestry industry.
